forks.actual: Backers’ consoles shipped from March 28, 2013 and were reviewed as a product in early April. Engadget said the system was “simply not ready for retail”; The Verge wrote that it was “being sold as a product, not a prototype, and that’s just wrong.”[^6][^7][^33] The retail launch followed on June 25, after a three-week delay the company attributed to demand.[^8][^10]
forks.whatif: Holding the backers’ units until the software and controller were finished would have broken the March promise on the Kickstarter page[^1] and cost months. It would also have meant the first reviews were of a finished machine. It would not have put more games on it.

forks.tab: Be a store, not a box
forks.actual: Ouya announced Ouya Everywhere in March 2014, nine months after launch, and reached its first outside device in July 2014.[^22] By the time it was for sale, the memo to investors pitched the catalogue, not the console: “the largest library of Android content for the TV.”[^24] Razer bought exactly that and left the hardware.[^25]
forks.whatif: Starting as a storefront and developer programme for other companies’ Android boxes would have spared the cost of making hardware. It would also have had no Kickstarter moment: the $99 box was what 58,224 backers (derived) paid for.[^1] A store with the same conversion rates on someone else’s box is not obviously a better business.

forks.actual: After its $15M round in 2013, Ouya “quietly secured some venture debt from TriplePoint Capital,” in Fortune’s words. A tripped covenant in 2015 put the company on the debtholder’s timetable, with expressions of interest due within the month.[^24]
forks.whatif: Without the loan there would have been no covenant to trip and no forced deadline, and Alibaba’s $10M might have bought a slower search for a partner.[^23] There would also have been less money to spend in 2013 and 2014. Since the amount borrowed was never disclosed, how much time it bought or cost is unknowable.
